title: The flaws in the blueprint of life
subtitle: Is genetic determinism misguided?
author: Omari Edwards
introduction: For twenty years, we’ve been promised that the key to who we are lies in our DNA. But as contributing editor Omari Edwards argues, the dream of a genetic blueprint has failed to deliver and may never have made sense to begin with. In one of the most anticipated debates at this year’s HowTheLightGetsIn London 2025 Festival, three pioneering thinkers, Denis Noble, Stuart Kauffman, and Joanna Moncrieff, will dismantle the myth of genetic determinism and clash over what should replace it. Is life encoded in our genes, or is the very idea of a biological script a scientific detour and a political danger?
body:
For two decades, we have been told that our genes are our destiny, the master script from which every trait, every strength, every flaw could be read. When the Human Genome Project was unveiled, it was hailed as the “blueprint of life,” a Rosetta Stone that would unlock the language of creation and deliver cures for the great diseases of our age. But the promised revolution never came. Beyond a handful of rare conditions, the hunt for simple genetic explanations has failed. The genome is not the manual for life we were promised. It remains a puzzle with missing pieces, its code shifting under the influence of environment, physiology, and chance.

Upcoming at HowTheLightGetsIn, three leading thinkers will ask whether the idea of a genetic blueprint has been a 20-year detour. Oxford biologist Denis Noble will set out how our genes are just ingredients, controlled by networks of feedback across the whole organism. Stuart Kauffman, the pioneer of complexity science, will insist that life is self-organising and creative, irreducible to any code. Psychiatrist Joanna Moncrieff will challenge not just the science but its politics, warning that genetic determinism risks turning human suffering into inherited defect while ignoring its social roots. Together they will clash over one of the biggest questions of modern science: Will the next revolution in biology redeem the genome’s promise or bury the dream of a genetic blueprint once and for all?

SUGGESTED VIEWING The agents of life With Johnjoe McFadden, Shini Somara, Denis Noble, Frances Ashcroft

What unites Denis Noble, Stuart Kauffman, and Joanna Moncrieff is their rejection of the old story: that the genome is a master plan from which our destiny can be read. Each of them dismantles that idea from a different angle; yet they disagree on what should replace it, and on how far we can go in building a new framework for biology and medicine.

The problem is not just that genetic determinism oversells what genes can do; it’s that it distorts how we think about life itself. It implies a one-way flow of causality, as if DNA were a script unrolling towards an inevitable future, when in reality genes are switched on and off by signals from cells, hormones, nutrition, and even mechanical forces in the body. Determinism flattens this complexity into a single code to be cracked, promising certainty where only probability exists. And that false promise shapes medicine, policy, and identity: it directs funding towards genome scans while underinvesting in prevention, and it encourages us to see health problems as personal flaws written in our DNA rather than as products of shared environments we might collectively change.

No master gene is pulling the strings.

Worse, genetic determinism has been used to prop up lazy and often harmful stereotypes. Claims that African runners are “genetically built” to dominate sprinting, or that certain ethnic groups are more intelligent or violent, are almost always based on cherry-picked data and poor science. Athletic success in Kenya’s Rift Valley, for example, is better explained by training regimes, altitude, and culture than by any single “running gene.” The same goes for IQ studies that claim racial gaps are innate while ignoring poverty, nutrition, and discrimination. Such arguments repackage old prejudices in the language of DNA and risk reviving the metaphysics of eugenics under a modern guise.

Stuart Kauffman, the pioneer of complexity science, insists that life’s patterns are emergent, not inscribed in our DNA. Genes, he argues, are enablers, not puppet-masters, and most of the interesting properties of living systems come from networks of interactions, not linear instructions. “No master gene is pulling the strings,” Kauffman argues, pointing to genome-wide studies that show only a faint genetic signal for most common diseases. The solution, in his view, lies in studying how order and novelty arise from interactions - from metabolic webs to ecological systems - even if that means accepting a level of unpredictability built into life itself.

Joanna Moncrieff takes a different tack. For her, genetic determinism is dangerous not only because it is scientifically weak, but because it risks moral and political harm. In psychiatry, she warns, the hunt for genetic causes can reframe social suffering as biological defect. The result is that poverty, trauma, and inequality are pushed out of view, while resources are poured into genetic screens of limited use. She does not deny biology’s role, but insists that genes must be understood within their social and psychological context. Where Kauffman sees complexity as a call for new science, Moncrieff sees it as a warning not to lose sight of lived experience.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Genes are not the blueprint for life With Denis Noble

Denis Noble, meanwhile, calls for a wholesale shift away from the blueprint metaphor, as in his panel with Richard Dawkins. Genes, he says, are more like ingredients in a recipe than lines in an architect’s plan. They do nothing on their own, and their effects are shaped by feedback from cells, organs, and environments. Causality in biology, Noble argues, is not one-way but circular: physiology and environment tell genes what to do as much as genes tell cells what to build. His vision is not to abandon genomics, but to integrate it into a systems view that reads life as a dynamic score rather than a static code.

This appeal to determinism often slips from science into doctrine and dogma.

Taken together, these three positions point in the same direction: away from the idea that life is fully scripted in our DNA. Yet they do not converge on a single answer. Kauffman emphasizes emergence and unpredictability, Noble calls for a symphonic model of control across scales, and Moncrieff demands that we keep the social causes of suffering at the center of the picture. The result is not a consensus but a fascinating, unresolved argument one that asks whether we can ever produce a single, unified theory of life, or whether complexity means there will never be a final blueprint to find.

But how did we end up here? What about the blueprint of life story was so appealing that we thought genes alone could be the solution to so many problems? Genetic determinism, an off shoot of a biological deterministic picture that our biology would give us all the answers, has long offered a seductive story: that our genome is a master script, and that if we could just decode it, we could predict and control the arc of our lives. The trouble is that this appeal to determinism often slips from science into doctrine and dogma. Instead of treating it as a testable claim, we have too often assumed it to be true by default, as though the idea that genes control us were something to accept on trust rather than to demonstrate with evidence.

Philosophers have given us a cleaner definition: a system is deterministic if, given its state at time t, its future is fixed by natural law. Applied to genetics, this would mean that if you knew an organism’s make up from the moment of conception, you could predict with near-certainty its future form and behaviour. Ned Block famously gave the example of five fingers: given the “right” genotype, almost everyone will develop five fingers. But even here, the determinism is partial; the awful thalidomide scandal  showed this. Exposure in utero to the drug can interrupt this “law,” and we are reminded that development is never perfectly shielded from other factors. A 100’000 babies were harmed by the use of the drug, and many thousands suffering debilitating malformations, and many more stillborn and miscarried children couldn’t fulfill the certainty their genes provided.

Stability comes in degrees, and for many of the outcomes we care most about, the degree is surprisingly low.

This is the heart of the problem. Some form of genetic determinism is strongest where the relationship is stable across all environments. But that stability is rare. For most traits, from mental illness to metabolic disorders to personality, the relationship is contingent, probabilistic, and mediated by everything from other genes to nutrition, pollution, and trauma. Philosopher James Woodward puts it bluntly: stability comes in degrees, and for many of the outcomes we care most about, the degree is surprisingly low.

Seen in this light, the cultural obsession with the genome as a “blueprint” looks less like science and more like metaphysics: yet another comforting story that there is a simple, universal language of life waiting to be read. This is where the HowTheLightGetsIn panel steps in, not to quibble over the details but to ask whether the whole paradigm is misguided.

This is why the cultural fantasy of a “simple language of life” is so dangerous. Metaphysics becomes science often reduces us to mere parishioners at the altar of science. Not to say that scientists themselves are priests, there is a reason the quote chosen for this panel is from Bill Clinton and not the scientists at the heart of this project. It reduces a staggeringly complex and interactive process to a single code to be cracked. It encourages us to look for “the gene for” everything and to ignore the wider biological and social web in which those genes operate. Worse, it fuels a technocratic dream that if we can just edit the code, we can fix the person, the population, even the species, an idea that edges disturbingly close to old-fashioned eugenics. Thankfully our panelists with their willingness to address the philosophical as well as scientific questions can challenge these malformed metaphysical commitments. If you’re around in London this weekend come join the debate.
